Instructions

Section titled “Instructions”
  • This quiz covers 1.1 Supply and Demand to 1.9 Information Economics and also uses present value and expected value from Stage 0. It is worth 100 points and should take about 120 minutes; each question shows its points.
  • You may use a calculator or code, but do not look at the lessons. The formulas you need are in the formula sheet below.
  • Show your working in calculation questions. Points are given for the working and the reasons; parts with only an answer and no working get no points. A true / false answer without a reason gets no points.
  • Write your answers on paper (or type them). When you are done, click “Copy scoring prompt” at the bottom of the page and send it with your answers to your AI assistant. You can also submit in several parts.

Questions

Section titled “Questions”
Part 1. True or false

Answer true or false, and give your reason. An answer without a reason gets no points.

Question 1 4 points
A 10-year investment product guarantees a nominal return of 2% a year (compounded annually), with principal and interest paid at maturity, and is advertised as "principal protected, you cannot lose money". If inflation is 3% in each of the 10 years, an investor who holds it to maturity has not lost purchasing power.
Question 2 7 points
Two consumers have different preferences and different incomes, but they face the same prices for two goods, each has chosen the bundle that maximizes their utility within their budget and spends all of their income, and both are at an interior optimum (they buy both goods, and their indifference curves are smooth). Then after they have bought, no exchange of goods between them (in any amounts, at any ratio) can make both of them better off.
Question 3 6 points
Over the past five years, house prices and the number of home sales in a city have both risen sharply. This shows that the city's demand curve for housing slopes upward: the higher the price, the more housing people want to buy.
Question 4 5 points
If demand for a good is perfectly inelastic (the quantity demanded is the same at any price), a per-unit tax on it causes no deadweight loss.
Question 5 6 points
A factory has the production function Q=K0.5L0.5Q = K^{0.5}L^{0.5}Q=K0.5L0.5 (KKK is machines, LLL is workers); in the long run both inputs can be adjusted, and the factory has been producing with the cost-minimizing mix. Wages rise by 20% while the rental price of machines stays the same. Wages used to be exactly half of total cost, so the lowest total cost of producing the same output as before rises by 10%.
Part 2. Problems
Question 6 15 points
There are two kinds of company, half of each. A "good company" has existing assets worth 200 (million dollars), and a "bad company" has existing assets worth 40. Both kinds have a new project: investing 20 raises the company's value by 25 (a net present value of +5). Managers know which kind their company is and decide in the interest of the existing shareholders; outside investors cannot tell, know only that half are of each kind, and price new shares fairly given what they believe. The companies have no cash, so to invest they must first raise 20.

(a) Suppose investors believe that both kinds will issue new shares and price them accordingly. At what value will investors price a company that issues new shares (using its value after the investment)? What share of the company must the new shareholders receive? What is the value finally owned by the old shareholders of a good company? Will a good company issue new shares to invest? (8 points)

(b) If a good company can instead borrow 20 of risk-free debt (one period, ignoring interest, repaying 20 at the end), will it invest? Why does debt avoid the problem in (a)? (7 points)
Question 7 13 points
A company's value can be seen as the capital invested plus the present value of its future economic profit; the part above the capital invested is called the premium. Companies A and B are each expected to earn an economic profit (profit after all costs, including the opportunity cost of capital) of 10 (million dollars) at the end of next year. A's industry has free entry; B has strong barriers to entry, and its economic profit is expected to stay at 10 every year forever. The discount rate is 8%.

(a) An analyst expects A's economic profit to start at 10 next year and then fall by 30% each year from the previous year (7 the year after, and so on). On his forecast, what should the premiums of A and B be? (5 points)

(b) The market currently gives A a premium of 50. At an 8% discount rate, how fast does the market price imply that A's economic profit falls each year? Are the analyst's expectation (a 30% fall each year) and the market's both consistent with "A's industry has free entry"? Can free entry alone tell which is closer to reality? Explain. (8 points)
Question 8 15 points
A client has 200,000 dollars in cash, which is all of her financial assets; she also has a fixed-rate mortgage at 4% with a balance of 200,000 dollars. Her financial adviser charges 1% a year of the assets he manages. He advises her not to pay off the mortgage but to let him invest the 200,000 dollars in a stock portfolio: "This portfolio has an expected return of 7% a year, higher than the 4% mortgage rate, so investing pays more." The standard deviation of the portfolio's yearly return is 15%. The client has CRRA utility with a coefficient of relative risk aversion γ=3\gamma = 3γ=3; when computing the risk premium, treat the 200,000 dollars as her wealth. The fee is deducted from the return at the end of the year. Paying off the mortgage is equivalent to a certain return of 4% a year. Compare one year only and ignore taxes.

(a) Evaluate the adviser's advice: which choice is better for this client? (11 points)

(b) If the adviser instead charged a fixed fee of 2,000 dollars a year, whatever the client chooses, would his advice still lean toward investing? What new problem could this way of charging create? (4 points)
Question 9 13 points
An industry has nnn identical firms with identical products, competing on price as in the Bertrand model, with the same marginal cost. If all firms set the monopoly price, the industry's total yearly profit is π\piπ, split equally among the nnn firms. Any firm that sets its price slightly below the others' captures almost the whole industry profit π\piπ for that year. The firms use trigger strategies: once anyone has cut the price, all firms price at marginal cost forever. The yearly discount factor is δ\deltaδ.

(a) Find the smallest δ\deltaδ that sustains collusion (in terms of nnn). What is it for n=2n = 2n=2? (6 points)

(b) Let δ=0.92\delta = 0.92δ=0.92. At most how many firms can there be for collusion to be sustained? Use this result to explain why antitrust authorities are more watchful of industries with few firms. (7 points)
Question 10 16 points
A perfectly competitive industry has market demand Qd=1000−10PQ_d = 1000 - 10PQd​=1000−10P. In the short run the number of firms is fixed and market supply is Qs=40P−1000Q_s = 40P - 1000Qs​=40P−1000. In the long run firms can enter and exit freely, all firms have the same costs, and changes in the size of the industry do not affect input prices (a constant-cost industry). The minimum of long-run average cost is 40, so long-run supply is a horizontal line at a price of 40. The industry is currently in long-run equilibrium. The government imposes a tax of 6 dollars per unit, paid by the firms.

(a) In the short run, what are the price buyers pay, the price firms receive and the quantity traded? How is the burden of the tax split? (5 points)

(b) What happens in the long run? Find the long-run price buyers pay and the quantity traded. Someone says: "This tax is levied on companies, so in the end it is borne by their shareholders." Evaluate this statement. (11 points)
